title: EIGHTH REPORT: You Can’t See Everything at Alpha
author: Benjamin Riley
summary: In the eighth installment of his investigation into Alpha School, the AI-driven private school network, Benjamin Riley turns from student experience to the organization's leadership. Drawing on multiple sources and LinkedIn cross-checks, he reconstructs an unofficial org chart centered on CEO Joe Liemandt, who funds the enterprise, directs its pedagogy by enthusiasm, and, according to sources, runs a culture of metrics-driven optimization with employee monitoring and high turnover. He profiles MacKenzie Price, Bill Ackman's reported shadow influence over the New York campus, Eliot Gattegno, Chris Just and several heads of schools, academics, expansion and communications. He also reports on 17 'waitlisted' campuses that sources say are on internal probation, and on a tangled corporate structure surfaced by an IXL lawsuit that points to Kaxxa Holdings as a parent entity. Riley argues that Liemandt's claim that Alpha uses Direct Instruction is contradicted by the guide role, which discourages teaching, and he closes with a public challenge to Liemandt for a recorded interview. The piece is advocacy journalism with named and anonymous sourcing, so claims are the author's reporting rather than adjudicated fact.
points: Alpha's leadership is concentrated in one funder-CEO, Joe Liemandt, and sources describe programming that lurches toward whatever he most recently read or heard.
Reported employee-side practices (KPI-driven optimization, keystroke logging, photos every 10 minutes, high turnover) mirror the extrinsic-motivation model applied to students.
The 'waitlist' label allegedly masks 17 campuses placed on internal probation for failing Alpha's '3 C's' commitments, with Price reportedly deciding when they exit.
Informal power matters as much as titles: Ackman is described as a 'shadow' lead of the NYC campus and Gattegno as Liemandt's chief-of-staff-like eyes and ears.
Alpha's layered corporate structure (Alpha Holdings, Kaxxa, ESW Capital, Crossover) makes accountability and employer identity hard to establish.
quotes: One thing is universally agreed upon by my sources: Joe Liemandt runs Alpha School. The buck stops with him. And the buck also starts with him, too — by all accounts, he is the primary if not exclusive funder of Alpha School’s operations.

What’s definitely true, and as I’ve previously reported, is that Liemandt believes deeply in the power of extrinsic motivation, using rewards and punishments not only to motivate students, but also his own employees.

Multiple sources describe to me a corporate culture of almost relentless “optimization,” where metrics and key performance indicators rule the day, and woe be the leaders or divisions that don’t hit theirs. Employee sources also describe being monitored much in the same way as students, with keystrokes logged and pictures taken of employees at regular 10-minute intervals to affirm they are in front of their screens.

This designation suggests these campuses are oversubscribed for enrollment. But multiple sources tell me this is not true, and that instead, the waitlisted campuses are essentially on internal probation for various reasons, including failing to satisfy Alpha’s “3 C’s,” the organization’s three core commitments to families

Sources tell me this goes beyond mere suggestions, and that if he wants something to happen, lower-level staff there feel obliged to follow his direction. According to my sources, this has created a significant degree of internal staff tension.

As a private commercial enterprise, Alpha School does not publish an organization chart, nor is it obligated to. Alpha School also does many different things and job titles are quite varied, even for roles that sources say are of equal leadership authority.
Multiple sources have said to me that Joe Liemandt will get excited by something he reads or listens to, and then Alpha will hurriedly orient programming around whatever this new interest is
